facts.claim: Gravity's pull on a falling climber, a rope or falling ice: standard gravity.

versions.note: Defined by ISO 80000-3; the real pull is about 0.5% greater at the poles than at the equator.

source.title: Wikipedia: Standard gravity

facts.claim: How hard snow holds a body sliding over it in ski clothing, the coefficient of kinetic friction: the game uses it for a climber sliding after a slip, and for a rope lying on the ground.

versions.note: Three fabrics on snow, a ski overall and two race suits, on a linear tribometer: dry friction, highest on the roughest fabric.

source.title: Nachbauer et al. 2016, Kinetic Friction of Sport Fabrics on Snow (Lubricants) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradients, the rise over the run, on which the energy cost of walking was measured: from 0.45 m down to 0.45 m up for each metre across, about 24°.

versions.note: Ten runners on a treadmill, walking and running at gradients from −0.45 to +0.45.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking on the level costs, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked, at the speed that makes it least.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking up the steepest gradient measured, +0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking down the steepest gradient measured, −0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: a fifth of the way up it.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The least energy walking costs on any gradient, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: on a gentle way down, technique.walking-cost-least-gradient, half the level's.

versions.note: Reduced to 0.81 ± 0.37 J/kg/m at −0.10.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradient on which walking costs least: 0.10 m down for each metre across, about 6°.

versions.note: The cost is reduced to its least at −0.10.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: Steeper than this gradient, up or down, walking works the muscles at the efficiency of their contraction, concentric up and eccentric down: the work against gravity is most of the cost, so each metre of height costs about the same however steep. The game takes it from 0.15 up, and from the steepest measured down.

versions.note: The mechanical efficiencies of walking and running above +0.15 and below −0.15 attained those of concentric and eccentric muscular contraction.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The power a fresh typical client at sea level, at a steady pace and carrying nothing, walks on, in watts for each kilogram they move: the body scales it by the capacity the altitude leaves, 60% at 5,000 m, and by the pack, and a step goes as fast as it pays for on the ground's gradient (technique.walking-cost-*). Fitted with the fastest walk and the ladder speeds so that a steady first crossing of the Icefall, drawn at 1/12 of its length (route.drawn-scale) with its walls and crevasses at life size, takes about 3.8 hours with the climb eased (technique.uphill-cost-share), the faster half of the 3–7 the sources give, by a climber who never stops at an anchor but steadies themselves on blue ice and the long ladders (#190): 3.78.

The fastest a climber walks in crampons, in metres a second, whatever power they have to spare: down a slope and on the flat their footing holds them to it, so their steps take less of their power and tire them less. Fitted with the walking power and the ladder speeds so that the way down the Icefall takes about 2.5 hours, the 4 from Camp 2 to Base Camp shared between the Icefall and the Western Cwm as the way up's 5 and 3 are: 2.9, with the climb eased (technique.uphill-cost-share) and the careful steps on ice and ladders (#190), 3.0 with a clip at each anchor on the way (#278); 3.2 once the walls' ladders are climbed down no faster than up them (#256). Faster, it barely shortens the way down, where most of the walking is held back by the stride's power on gentle ground, and the ladders drawn at life size take twelve times their real minutes either way while only the way up's walking is eased.

The share of the climb's extra cost, a metre up a slope over a metre on the level (technique.walking-cost-*), that a stride pays in the game: a playability tuning, not a measurement, so that the slopes between the ladders don't crawl (#186). Up a slope a stride pays the level's cost and this share of the rest, so a slope never goes faster than the level, and the steeper it is the more the climb is eased: twice as fast up 20°. Fitted so that a careful typical client who never stops at an anchor crosses the Icefall in about 3.8 hours, the faster half of the 3–7 the sources give: 3.78, with the veteran at the shortest, 3, and the novice at the middle, 5. A player stops at every anchor to clip, so their own crossing is longer.

Up to this steepness, snow never slips under a climber in crampons (#208); steeper, the chance a metre of it slips grows in a straight line to technique.slip-steep at the steepest ground walked. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, about 30°, where a slip ends badly, and to the Icefall's 20° slopes, walked without a thought.

The chance a metre of snow slips under a climber at the steepest ground walked without a ladder (route.icefall-steepness), at a steady pace and rested (#208): from technique.slip-free-steepness it grows in a straight line from none to this. A careful pace divides it and a hurried or tired one multiplies it (body.rest-step-footing). Fitted so that a careful climber slips on the Icefall's steep snow now and then, and the rope, clipped, holds them: the lesson is the rope's.

How fast that fresh climber at sea level crosses a ladder laid flat over a crevasse, in metres a second. The ladders are drawn at life size on a section drawn at 1/12 (route.drawn-scale), so a ladder takes twelve times its real mountain minutes: fitted with the speeds up and down a wall so that the Icefall's twenty-one ladders, ten over crevasses and eleven up and down walls of 3 to 11 m, take about an hour and a half of the way up's hours together.

How fast that climber goes up a ladder stood against a wall, in metres a second; between flat and vertical, the speed falls in a straight line over the sine of the ladder's angle. Fitted with the crossing speed to the Icefall's hours.

How much slower a climber goes down a ladder than up it at their own pace, as a share of the speed up: the game comes down a wall's ladder at the speed up it less this share, where the footing holds them back (#256). Nothing makes it quicker in crampons: no source measures them on rungs, and climbers tell of the points catching on them (technique.ladder-down-cost says why the breath holds them back less on the way down).

versions.note: Nineteen firefighters in their own work boots and gloves, with a 9 kg pack, up and down ladders at 30°, 52.5° and 75° at a self-selected normal pace, about 0.4 m/s: climbing down was 8.8% slower than climbing up (p = 0.0003).

source.title: Simeonov et al. 2020, Effects of Aerial Ladder Rung Spacing on Firefighter Climbing Biomechanics (Applied Ergonomics) → 3.1 Climbing speed

facts.claim: What a metre down a ladder costs a climber, as a share of what a metre up it costs: the oxygen they take up descending against ascending. The game buys a climber's speed down a wall's ladder with their stride's power at this share of the cost up it, so the altitude and tiredness slow them less on the way down, and the rungs take only a share of their power where their footing holds them back (#256).

versions.note: Kamon 1970, as the review cites it: oxygen uptake 26% lower descending a ladder ergometer than ascending it.

source.title: Milligan, O'Halloran and Tipton, An Ergonomics Assessment of Three Simulated 120 m Ladder Ascents (University of Portsmouth) → Introduction

versions.note: Barron et al. 2017, as the review cites it: oxygen uptake 46% lower descending a 30 m vertical ladder than in its ascent of 3 min 45 s; a share by the minute, the descent's time not given.

source.title: Milligan, O'Halloran and Tipton, An Ergonomics Assessment of Three Simulated 120 m Ladder Ascents (University of Portsmouth) → Introduction

facts.claim: The chance a metre climbed on a ladder slips, at a steady pace and rested, before a crossing's bounce (#208): a crampon placed carelessly on an aluminium rung skates off it. Fitted so that a careful crossing rarely slips on the rungs alone, and the fall from a ladder in 2012 (route.icefall-lessons) needs carelessness or a bounce.

The chance a metre of blue ice on the level slips under a climber at a steady pace, rested (#208): bare ice holds a crampon's points less than snow, and a careless step skates on it. Fitted so that a climber at a steady pace on the Icefall's blue ice slips about once a crossing, and one at the rest step a few times less often.

How much more likely a metre of blue ice is to slip for each unit of the sine of its slope, up or down (#208): a slope of ice is worse than a flat of it, and a ramp of it down to a crevasse's lip is the worst of the Icefall.

How hard bare blue ice holds a body sliding on it, as technique.snow-friction is snow's (#190): a slip on ice slides on where one on snow would stop. Fitted so that a slip on a gentle slope of ice ends in the crevasse below it unless a rope holds the climber.

How much a ladder across a crevasse bounces for each metre walked on it and each metre of its length (#190): a long one, lashed from three or four, sinks in the middle and bounces. It dies away (technique.ladder-bounce-damp), and takes footing from whoever is on it (technique.ladder-bounce-loss). Fitted so that a steady pace across a ladder of three sections, about 8 m, slips halfway over, the rest step crosses it, and two on it at once bounce it twice as hard.
The share of a ladder's bounce that dies away a second once nobody steps on it (#190): a ladder settles in about three seconds. Fitted with technique.ladder-bounce-excite.

How much each unit of a ladder's bounce adds to the chance a metre on it slips (#208). Fitted with technique.ladder-bounce-excite so that a hurried crossing of a long ladder, bouncing hard, slips more often than not, and a careful one rarely.

The share of the bounce a ladder across a crevasse takes from the steps on it while someone stands at one of its ends holding its line taut (#212), as a client's Sherpa does from the far side: held, a lashed ladder sinks and sways less, and a careful crossing slips less.
In the Icefall a client's own Sherpa leads: he sets the pace and looks back, crosses each ladder first, and holds its line taut from the far side while the client crosses.

versions.note: The client's Sherpa goes ahead through the Icefall, crosses each ladder first and keeps the safety line taut from the far side for the client.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2018: Into the Icefall

versions.note: A first trip through the Icefall: the Sherpa leads and sets the pace, and each ladder is crossed one climber at a time, the line held from the other side.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Virtual Everest 2020: First Steps in the Khumbu Icefall

facts.claim: A client's personal Sherpa climbs beside them on all their climbs to the camps; on summit day a climbing Sherpa goes just behind them.

versions.note: The personal sherpa climbs beside the member on all climbs to the camps.

source.title: Project Himalaya: Trek and climb job roles

facts.claim: A climber who slips off a ladder and hangs over the crevasse on its line is pulled out by whoever is nearest, then sits a while on safe ground to recover before going on.

versions.note: A slip off a ladder in the Icefall left the climber hanging over the crevasse on the safety line until a teammate pulled him out.

source.title: Allan Meek: Falling down an Everest ice crevasse (2017)

facts.claim: How far ahead of the first of his clients a Sherpa walks in the Icefall, in the slope's metres as the game draws them (#212): he walks on when they come nearer than the least of it and waits once he's the most of it ahead, near enough to look back and talk, and to reach each ladder first.

How far the last of his clients may fall behind a Sherpa before he stops and waits for them, in the slope's metres (#212); he never waits under the seracs or on a snow bridge, but past them, as the Icefall is crossed without lingering where the ice falls.
How far behind a client who goes ahead of him a Sherpa follows, in the slope's metres (#212): he closes up when they're the most of it ahead and stops when they're nearer than the least.

The mountain's minutes a Sherpa sits with a client he has pulled off the rope, on safe ground, before they go on (#212): long enough to get their breath back, and short enough not to lose the cold of the morning.

The speed a falling climber hits the ice at, in metres a second, past which the fall kills them (#190): a drop of about 7 m through the air onto ice. Fitted so that a fall into one of the Icefall's crevasses, over 45 m deep in places (route.icefall-hazards), kills, as the fifteen-storey fall from a ladder near Camp 1 did in 2012 (accidents.2012-ladder-fall), and a slip down a few metres of a wall's foot doesn't.

How fast a fresh climber at sea level, hanging on a fixed rope after a slip off a ladder or over a lip, climbs back up to where they slipped, in metres a second, at a whole stride (#190): hand over hand on the rope and the ladder's rails, crampons on the ice. Fitted so that climbing back the metre or two a clipped slip leaves them below takes a minute or two of the mountain's time, and tires them.

How many of the mountain's seconds a ladder staged to break creaks and shifts under a climber before it breaks (#209), and one sliding off its lip under two before it falls (#256): long enough to clip in, a second and a quarter of play at the mountain's pace (time.compression). The moving glacier shifts and drops ladders (route.icefall-hazards).

The Icefall Doctors ask every climber in the Khumbu Icefall to cross its ladders one at a time, and the high-altitude workers to carry lighter loads so as not to overload them: the game's coach says so at a ladder someone is on, its Sherpa never steps onto one, and a ladder with two on it can slide off its lip (#256).

versions.note: Among the precautions the Ice Doctors ask of everyone when the route opened: only one climber on any ladder at a time; lighter loads for the high-altitude workers, to avoid overloading the ladders; harnesses clipped to the safety ropes on the ladders.

source.title: Explorersweb: Everest: Icefall Open but Climbers Advised to Hurry Through It (18 April 2024)

facts.claim: On 9 May 2018 two Sherpas fell into a crevasse in the Icefall when the ladders they were crossing gave way: the ladder lay too near the crevasse's edge, and as the second Sherpa stepped onto it, its end slid in and took them both down. They were clipped to the safety lines, which held them, and neither was hurt.

versions.note: Filmed by Nobukazu Kuriki's crew. The clipped safety lines probably prevented a disaster; the ladders are adjusted daily, the Icefall always moving.

source.title: Snowbrains: VIDEO: Sherpas Fall in to Crevasse on Everest when Ladder Collapses Beneath Them (17 May 2018)

facts.claim: The chance that a ladder across a crevasse slides off its lip as a climber steps onto it with someone already on it (#256), as one did under a second Sherpa in 2018 (technique.ladder-slid-in): it creaks, then falls with whoever is on it, the end they stepped on from torn free, and the ropes hold those clipped. No source counts how often a shared crossing ends so: a playability choice that makes the Icefall Doctors' rule (technique.one-on-a-ladder) matter without making every shared crossing a fall, about one in ten.

The minutes two climbers at its lips take to haul a ladder that broke and fell into its crevasse back up by its ropes and lash it across again (#228), pulling together at a whole stride each: the sections lashed end to end with rope (route.icefall-ladders-lashed) come up slowly hand over hand, and the lashings and anchors take their time. One alone can't lift it; nobody comes to fix it for them.

How fast a partner at the lip hauls a climber hanging on the rope back up it, at a whole stride (#209): as fast as the climber climbs back alone (technique.climb-back-speed), so the two of them together come up twice as fast, and one who can't climb still comes out.
How near the point a hanging climber is hauled up to their partner has to stand to haul them (#209): at the lip above them, on the safety line (route.icefall-ladders-lashed).

The minutes on the move after which a crampon not checked before setting off comes loose, on the next ladder (#196): a skipped check catches up with the climber about an hour out of Base Camp, not at once, as the fall from a ladder near Camp 1 in 2012 began with a crampon caught on a rung (accidents.2012-ladder-fall).

How sure-footed a loose crampon leaves a climber, as a share of what they'd be with it strapped tight (#196): their chance of slipping on blue ice, a ladder or steep snow is divided by it, three times as likely, until they kneel to refit it.
The minutes a climber takes to kneel and refit a loose crampon, its straps tightened again, standing on the ground (#196).

The hours after setting off at which a headlamp without fresh batteries dies (#196): from the 3 a.m. start (time.base-camp-departure), the climber goes on by starlight until dawn, the ice and the crevasses' lips unlit.

How sure-footed a climber is in the dark without a headlamp, as a share of what they'd be by its light (#196): they can't see where they put their crampons on the ice and the rungs, so their chance of slipping is twice what it would be, unless they slow down or wait for first light (time.first-light).
On Everest, climbers who had climbed on another peak of Nepal before summit more often than those who hadn't, and die no less often.

versions.note: 67.6% against 61.5% summited in 2006–2019, an advantage that has about halved in 25 years; deaths, the descent's too, independent of experience. The database records earlier Nepalese and border peaks, not other mountains.

source.title: Huey et al. 2020, Mountaineers on Mount Everest: Effects of age, sex, experience, and crowding on rates of success and death (PLoS One) → Results

facts.claim: The share of the speed on a ladder and clipped to a fixed rope of a climber who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder, against one with alpine climbs behind them, whom the ladder speeds and the walking power are fitted to. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, takes about the middle of the hours the sources give a first crossing of the Icefall, 5, where a typical client who never stops at an anchor takes 3.8: 5.0. Stopping at each anchor for their clips, as the stories' careful walker does, they took 4.3 and 5.5 before #256; since, they also wait their turn at the ladders Pemba is on and climb the walls' ladders down no faster than up them: the typical client takes 4.8 and the novice 5.9, near the 6 the sources give foreigners on a first rotation.

The same share for a climber who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, crosses the Icefall the first time in about 3 hours, the shortest the sources give it, and summits more often: they take less time on the ropes, not fewer risks (technique.experience-and-summits).

How far a cowstail reaches from the climber's harness to the fixed rope, in metres: how far from the rope they can clip, and how far past an anchor the rope lets them. Fitted so that a climber beside a ladder can reach the rope fixed along it.

How fast falling ice, an avalanche or a breaking snow bridge throws a climber it catches down the slope, in metres a second: a fall their rope holds if they're clipped. Fitted so that an unroped climber caught on a slope slides off it.

The fastest slide a climber can stop with the ice axe driven into the slope, in metres a second: self-arrest works in a slide's first moments or not at all. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, where a slip not stopped at once ends badly.
How far from their body a sliding climber can drive the ice axe into the slope, in metres: an arm and the axe. Fitted with the arrest speed to the Lhotse Face.

facts.question: At an anchor where one fixed rope ends and the next begins, in what order does a climber move their cowstails across, and are they ever clipped to neither rope?

How do climbers on the South route rig their cowstails: the jumar on one and a carabiner on the other, and how long is each, so how far can a climber reach to clip? The game gives a cowstail 0.8 m of reach.

How does a climber cross a ladder laid over a crevasse in the Icefall: clipped to what, stepping how in crampons, and how fast? The game crosses at 0.6 m/s at sea level, less at altitude, and a long ladder bounces under a hurried step until the climber loses their footing.

How does a climber go up a ladder stood against an ice wall, and down it: clipped to what, facing it or not, and what holds a slip? Down it, do clients climb the rungs, or go down the rope beside it on a descender or an arm wrap? The game climbs at 0.3 m/s at sea level, slower at altitude, and climbs down the rungs 8.8% slower than that, as firefighters did, its altitude slowing them less (#256).
How does a climber go up a fixed rope on a jumar, on the Lhotse Face for instance: the rhythm of hand, feet and breath, and when does the second cowstail move?

How does a climber go down a fixed rope: abseiling on a belay device, with the rope wrapped round an arm, or on the carabiner alone, and where on the South route is each used? How fast does a client abseil a step of ice a few metres high in the Icefall?
What is the rest step, with its rhythm of steps and breaths, and how does the rhythm change with altitude and with bottled oxygen?
On hard, steep ice such as the Lhotse Face, where a fixed rope is in place: how are the crampons placed, on the front points or flat-footed, and when does the ice axe go in?

How fast does a climber walk on ground of each steepness, up and down, in crampons and with a pack, and how much slower on a ladder? The game's walking costs what Minetti et al. measured on a treadmill, read as rise over run, from 24° down to 24° up, each metre of height costing the same past that up to 60°; a climber walks on 2.2 W/kg at sea level, before the altitude and the pack take their share, and no faster than 0.7 m/s whatever they have to spare. The power, the fastest walk and the ladder speeds up and across are fitted to the hours the sources give the Icefall, up and down, not measured; down a ladder goes 8.8% slower than up it and costs about two thirds of it, as firefighters and ladder ergometers measured at sea level (#256). How much slower are crampons on the rungs, going down?

How often does a climber slip on snow and ice of each steepness, and on a ladder, and how much does a careful pace help? At a steady pace the game gives snow no chance of a slip up to 30°, rising to 1 in 100 a metre at the Icefall's steepest; level blue ice 1 in 50 a metre, and twice that on a slope of 30°; a ladder's rungs about 1 in 330 a metre, more as it bounces under the steps; the rest step makes each four times less likely, and the faster pace about three times more (#208).

Up to what speed can a sliding climber stop themselves with the ice axe, on snow and on hard ice, and within how many seconds of the slip? How far from the body does the axe reach, and how hard do snow and hard ice hold a sliding climber without it? The game stops a slide no faster than 5 m/s, with the axe driven in within 1.5 m above the body, and never in the air; without the axe, a slide stops by itself only on ground gentler than about 19°, by the friction measured for ski fabrics on snow.

How much slower on the Icefall's ladders and fixed ropes is a client who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder than one with alpine climbs behind them, and how much faster one who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak? Do they slip more, or less, for each metre? The game fits their speed there to the spread of the sources' hours for a first crossing, and leaves their slips for each metre as they are: experience brings more summits, not fewer deaths.

facts.claim: How ice is climbed on crampons and tools: flat-footed, all points but the front ones in the ice, on low-angle to moderately steep ice; on steep ice by front pointing, on the front points of the crampons and the picks of the ice tools, each tool placement tested before it's trusted.

versions.note: French technique, flat-footing, is the preferred technique for slopes up to about 40°.

source.title: REI Expert Advice: How to Climb Ice

versions.note: The core technique for climbing steep ice is front pointing.

source.title: UKClimbing: Ice Climbing Technique

versions.note: A placement is tested by pulling down on it, slowly adding weight, and isn't trusted until then; the aim on fat ice is that every placement is solid.

source.title: Gripped: Tips for Safer and Warmer Ice Climbing This Winter

facts.claim: How climbers go down the fixed ropes: clipped to them with their carabiners from one section to the next, the rope wrapped round an arm where it's gentle, and through a figure-8 descender, rappelling, where it's steep.

versions.note: While descending, climbers secure their way with a lifeline and carabiners from section to section; depending on the steepness, they may just roll the rope around their arm or use a figure-8 descender to rappel down. The jumar's teeth stop it sliding back down the rope.

source.title: ExplorersWeb: Newcomers' Guide: Fixed Ropes in Himalayan Climbing (2022)

facts.claim: How fast a fresh climber at sea level lowers themselves down a step of ice too steep to walk, on the fixed rope that runs down it, through their descender, in metres a second, at a whole stride: their front points against the ice, their cowstails on the rope. Fitted so that the way down from Camp 1 keeps the hours the sources give it, the Icefall's steps of ice with no ladder rappelled about as fast as a ladder down them would be climbed.

How fast a fresh climber at sea level climbs ice too steep to walk on two ice tools and their front points, in metres a second, at a whole stride: a pick swung in, the feet walked up under it. Fitted with the Icefall's steps of ice, which have no ladder, to the hours the sources give the crossing: a step a few metres high takes some minutes of the mountain's time, longer than a ladder up it would, and longer still on the ice axe alone.
The share of that speed a climber makes on the ice axe alone, with no second tool: each move waits for the one pick to come out and go in again.
How high above their feet a climber's pick goes into the ice at full stretch, in metres up: an arm, the tool's shaft and their height. Their feet go no lower under a pick than this.
How far below a pick a climber's feet stop on the way up, in metres: locked off, the pick at their shoulder. To go higher they swing the next one in.
Above this height over their feet, in metres, a pick is swung at full stretch and bites poorly: the climber who over-reaches can't put their weight behind the swing.
How near the ice the player has to point for a pick to go in there, in metres: the aim the game asks of the hand.
How far past the lip of a face a pick is planted on the ground above it to top out, and how far past it the axe goes in when a climber steps down onto the face, in metres.

The chance that a metre climbed on steep ice slips, for a climber on two tools whose picks bite well: about one slip in 250 m. Fitted so that a careful climber rarely comes off a wall of the Icefall, and a careless one does.
How many times likelier a metre of steep ice slips on the ice axe alone than on two tools.
How many times likelier a metre of steep ice slips for a climber who hangs from a pick that bites poorly: swung at full stretch, or into brittle ice.

The chance that a swing comes off for a climber on the ice axe alone, who stands on their front points with no pick in the ice while it swings: about one swing in a hundred, more for one who is spent.
The share of a stride's power that hanging still on the ice tools takes: there's no rest on steep ice, only a slower way to tire.

facts.question: On the steep ice of the Icefall where there's a fixed rope and no ladder: how fast does a client climb it on the jumar, the axe and their front points, how often do they come off, and how much does a second ice tool change it? Do clients carry one there at all?

facts.claim: On snow and ice up to about 40° a climber in crampons stands and walks flat-footed, every point but the front ones in; steeper, on the front points, which tire the calves quickly, so that nobody stands there long.

versions.note: Flat-footing, the French technique, is the preferred technique on low-angle to moderately steep ice, slopes up to about 40°.

source.title: REI Expert Advice: How to Climb Ice

versions.note: Mountaineers avoid front-pointing as much as they can: it wears out the calves quickly.

source.title: Alpine Institute: Crampon Technique for Ice Climbing

facts.claim: At each anchor of the fixed line a climber clips the next rope before unclipping the last, one carabiner at a time, the jumar too: a clip-in takes about half a minute, and the anchors come often, so they add up; tired or new to it, a climber fumbles the carabiners.

versions.note: Skipping a clip-in to save 30 seconds across a small ladder section is the commonest contributor to fatal crevasse falls.

source.title: Global Summit Guide: Khumbu Icefall, the mistakes that have killed climbers since 2014

versions.note: Climbers swear at each anchor that makes them unclip the carabiner, perhaps the jumar, and at how close together the anchors are.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2013: Climbing to Camp 1

versions.note: Coming down through the Icefall there is no room for tired steps or fumbled carabiners.

source.title: RMI Expeditions: Mt. Everest Expedition: Ice Fall Dress Rehearsal (2011)

facts.claim: On the Icefall's fixed lines the Sherpas pass the clients, going up and coming down, and the client steps aside to let them by.

versions.note: As the traffic picks up, a client gets used to stepping aside to let Sherpas pass going up and coming down.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2013: Climbing to Camp 1

facts.claim: How long the typical client's hands take to clip one cowstail's carabiner onto a rope, standing (#197): a changeover clips two, the half a minute a clip-in takes; a climber's technique shares it as it shares their speed, so a novice is slower at the anchors and a veteran quicker.

The chance a second a climber standing still on their front points slips, at a steady pace's sure-footedness (#197): on a face of ice, or on blue ice too steep to stand on flat-footed, the calves tire, the more on the axe alone and on a pick that bites poorly. Fitted so that a minute's stand there on the axe alone slips a climber about one time in twenty, and a clip's seconds seldom: they climb on, or rest on the rope, which takes their weight.

The chance a second a climber standing still on a ladder slips, for each unit of its bounce past what a careful crossing sets going on its own (#197): a lashed ladder lurches in three dimensions under someone else's steps. Fitted so that a climber standing on a long ladder while another hurries onto it slips now and then, and never from their own crossing's sway.

How hard a ladder bounces, in technique.ladder-bounce-excite's units, before a climber standing still on it can slip (#197): a careful crossing of the Icefall's longest ladder sways it about this hard on its own, and another's hurried steps past it.

The share of a jolt's chance of slipping a climber, a gust, a ladder twisting, someone passing them on the rope (#197), that is left when they stand still, braced for it, against one on the move: the warning's point is to stop.
How near along the ground one climber passes another on a rope they share for the passing to jolt the one passed (#197): within arm's reach.

The chance a climber passed on the rope slips, on the move where a slip can happen, at a steady pace's sure-footedness (#197): the passer brushes by, the rope tugs. Fitted so that a client standing aside on blue ice or a ladder's end is seldom upset, and one walking on careless more often.

How many of the mountain's seconds a client who went ahead of their Sherpa stands still before he goes past them on the fixed rope to lead again (#197): a couple of minutes' rest, and he steps by, as the Sherpas pass their clients going up and down.

A crevasse rescue goes in this order: an anchor of two pieces in the snow or the ice, the second equalised with the first; to the lip, to see whether the partner answers; the lip cleared and padded; and the haul. A partner who doesn't answer is reached by rappelling down into the crevasse.

versions.note: The first piece is very strong, the second equalised with it by a sling or a cordelette; at the lip the rescuer checks the partner is conscious, clears and pads the lip, and hauls on a 3:1; if the partner doesn't answer, the rescuer has to rappel down into the crevasse.

source.title: American Alpine Institute: Crevasse Rescue, an introduction

facts.claim: On the simple haul system of a crevasse rescue, the Z-pulley, the rescuer pulls this many metres of rope for each metre the casualty rises, and bears a third of their weight; it's used wherever it can be, being the fastest.

versions.note: For every 3 feet pulled, the victim rises 1 foot; the 3:1 is used whenever possible because it's faster than the 6:1.

source.title: American Alpine Institute: Crevasse Rescue, an introduction

versions.note: The simple haul system: the victim's weight divided by 3, quick and simple to set up, suited to a victim who can help on the wall or is light enough; a victim who can't help, or a heavy one, takes the double Mariner, 7 to 1, and a lot of rope.

source.title: Petzl: Crevasse rescue no. 3, haul systems for crevasse rescue

facts.claim: The mountain's minutes a rescuer at a whole stride takes to build the anchor of a rescue line at a crevasse's lip and throw the rope down (#241): two ice screws, equalised, the lip cleared and padded (technique.crevasse-rescue-order).

How fast a rescuer at a whole stride hauls a casualty who can't help up a rescue line on its pulleys, in metres a second (#241): a third of the haul of a partner who climbs with them (technique.haul-speed), three metres of rope pulled for each one risen (technique.haul-three-to-one).
How near a casualty a rescuer kneels to treat them or to take them onto their back, in metres (#241): within arm's reach of where they lie.
The mountain's minutes it takes to get a casualty onto a rescuer's back, tied on with a sling for the carry, or to set them down off it (#241).

The share of their stride a rescuer keeps with a casualty on their back (#241). Fitted to the rescue of 18 May 2023, when Gelje Sherpa and those who helped him brought a climber 600 m down from the Balcony in about six hours, dragged on the snow or carried in turns on their backs (sherpas.carried-down-metres, sherpas.carried-down-hours): a third of a pace, on the Icefall's lower, thicker air.

facts.question: Does one Sherpa alone haul a casualty who can't help out of a crevasse on a 3:1, or does he rig the double Mariner (technique.haul-three-to-one) or wait for more hands? And how is a casualty with a broken leg carried through the Icefall's ladders: on the back, in a rope seat, on a sled, lowered at each step?
